questions.title: What are the requirements for a non-defendant third party to validly consent to a search of a home?
questions.question_body: I'm working through the Ninth Circuit precedent here, but I'm finding the text confusing because the Fifth Circuit decided *Cellitti* c.o. 2nd Cir., which the Seventh Circuit is citing. Specifically, *Matlock* says a third party might consent in places where both she and the defendant have 'legitimate expectations of privacy'. In this case, the wife is consenting for the husband. Does the wife need to own a piece of the crime or control the premises, or can she consent based solely on shared privacy expectations?

questions.title: I don't understand how the phrase 'almost need to come inside' avoids violating the voluntariness standard.
questions.question_body: The officer says 'I'm sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure of that.' I thought telling someone they 'need' to do something for the court to get into the room qualifies as coercion under *Bumper v. North Carolina*. The district court said there was no coercion, but the appellate court deferred. Can someone explain why the district court's finding on these facts was enough to avoid a clear error standard?

questions.title: Why did the court treat the officers' initial entry as a search warrantless entry rather than an exigent situation if they found a gun?
questions.question_body: I see the officers entered based on consent, but then they got a warrant based on information inside later. Why isn't this an application of the 'exigent circumstances' doctrine for officer safety instead? The court explicitly says the consent is sufficient. Can someone explain why they didn't focus more on the 'protective sweep' or 'hot pursuit' aspect of the warrantless entry?

questions.title: What is the specific scope of consent when the officers wanted to check on children's safety?
questions.question_body: The pretext for entry was 'checking the welfare of her children.' However, they scanned the home, asked about the dogs, located Coleman in a separate bedroom, and found firearms. Is there a bright line separation where consented to 'checking kids' would never include 'locating guns in back rooms'? How does the court determine if the subsequent search of the home fits within the initial 'checking' scope?

questions.title: How does the 'objective reasonableness' standard apply when a defendant challenges the scope of consent?
questions.question_body: I read that the standard for reviewing the officer's idea of what 'typical reasonable person would understand' is 'objective reasonableness'. However, the text says the proper inquiry for evaluating the scope of consent is 'what would the typical reasonable person have understood'. Is that the defendant's burden to challenge where their expectation of privacy was not objectively reasonable, or is the court just asking if a reasonable person would have understood the objective complaint from the officers?

questions.title: Why did the Seventh Circuit adopt a 'clear error' review standard for the District Court's finding of consent?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, they say, 'We review a district court's finding of voluntary consent... for clear error.' But how does that differ from the 'de novo' review standard for legal questions or 'abuse of discretion' for factual findings in 4th Amendment cases? Is the error standard dependent on whether it is a constitutional issue or a Fourth Amendment procedural issue? I am confused about why a constitutional hardship like consensual entry gets clear error review.
